utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone here in The Hague, and good morning to those who are at the location of the videolink. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Could I ask whether the representative of the Registry at the videolink location could hear me and can see me?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Good morning, Your Honours -- or good afternoon. I can hear you, but unfortunately I cannot see you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any way that we could check the video connection?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Your Honour, I believe the technicians have been trying to make it work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber has considered whether we could continue where the -- at the videolink location no one can see us and where we can see, however, all the persons at the videolink location. The Chamber decided that we need a full two-way video and audio in order to proceed, and for that reason we briefly adjourn again and we'll wait and see whether the full dual communication is restored soon. We take another break. --- Break taken at 1.18 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume the court session, and I again wish a good morning to the representative of the Registry at the other side of the videolink, the videolink location. And could I inquire whether you now can see us and hear us?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Hi, good morning, again, Your Honours. Yes, I can hear you and I can see you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then we will proceed. I do understand that two representatives of the Canadian government will be present. Could they be escorted into the videolink room to start with.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Yes, immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Ms. Wickler and Ms. Soliman. You were with us in The Hague last week. The same instructions apply as I gave them at that moment; that is, you can intervene if there is any state security concern, but apart from that you are supposed to refrain from any intervention in the examination of the witness. I see you're nodding, and since you understood that last week, I take it that you understand it this week as well. Welcome into the videolink location. Then could the witness be escorted into the videolink room. I would urge the parties to see whether it will be possible to conclude the testimony of the witness today, because it's not foreseen that we would continue tomorrow, and the hour we lost today might still enable us to finish today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Gauthier. Can you see me, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please stand because the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration, the text of which is now handed out to you. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gauthier. Please be seated. Mr. Gauthier, you'll first be examined by the party that called you, by Mr. Ivetic. Mr. Ivetic is a member of the Mladic Defence team. You'll see him in a second, I take it, when the camera is on him. Mr. Ivetic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Could I ask you to please kindly state your full name for purposes of the record.

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: Michel Joseph Camilien Gauthier.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, since we both will be seeking English today, I would ask that we observe a brief pause between question and answer. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, did you have occasion to give a written statement to the Defence team of Radovan Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would like to call up in e-court 1D03950, a copy of which you should have there with the court officer. And, sir, my first question is: Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we can turn together to page 4 of this document, here we see a signature and the date February 6th, 2012. Can you identify for us whose signature is on this page?

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: That is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, subsequent to signing this statement on the date indicated, did you have a chance to review the statement to see if any corrections are needed to the same?

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: To be honest, I did not review it for the purpose of considering whether it needed to be corrected. So do you wish me to do that now?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If you could, sir --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We need to know --

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: I acknowledge that this is the statement that I provided the Karadzic Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Do you stand by everything as in your statement as being accurate?

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: Yes, to the best of my recollection at the time I signed the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, today if I were to ask you questions arising out of the same material as contained in your written statement, would your answers to those questions today be in substance the same as recorded in your statement?

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: I suppose that would depend on the context of the question -- within the question was put, but in principle, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, today you have now taken a solemn declaration. Does that mean we can consider the material in your statement to be truthful in nature?

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would tender 1D03950 as a public exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we could actually just leave it MFI'd, and maybe if on the first break if General Gauthier could take a look at the statement and just let us know if there is any corrections and provided that -- whatever the response is, then decide on admission at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think that's prudent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I was about to suggest the same as a matter of fact. Mr. Gauthier, you're invited during the first break to read again your statement. And if there would be any need to make any corrections that you tell us after the break. Meanwhile, in view of the fact that you said that this is the statement you gave and that you gave the answers to the -- in accordance with the truth to the best of your recollection, that we consider that there may be little chance that you would like to correct something. But if you would do so, then please do it after the first break. Meanwhile, we'll mark your statement for identification, which is a step in between -- in between tendering and admission. Madam Registrar, the number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D03950 receives Exhibit Number D1242.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is for the time being marked for identification. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time I would like to read a short summary of the statement for purposes of the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant General Gauthier is a retired Canadian army officer deployed two times to the former Yugoslavia as a member of UNPROFOR. From September 1993 to August 1994, he was the UNPROFOR force engineer stationed at UNPROFOR headquarters in Zagreb. He was a colonel at that time. After an explosion killed and wounded a large number of people at the Markale market on 5 February 1994, he was assigned to a United Nations investigation into the incident in question. He was the team leader of that investigation. They were told to confine their investigation to crater analysis and the related technical aspects of the explosion. His investigative team found that the initial French Battalion team used an unconventional method to determine bearing and thus their results were suspect. The French had also chipped away at the hole to excavate the tail fin and thus enlarged the crater hole. Likewise, the General's team determined Captain Verdy made a mathematical error in the second analysis of the crater. By the time the General's team did their investigation, six days had elapsed since the explosion. Based on the condition of the crater, they concluded the direction of fire to be anywhere between 330 and 420 mils from the point of detonation. Although they also tried to measure the angle of descent, due to the previous excavation of the crater and hole it was assessed that the results were not sufficiently accurate to be used as a basis for a finding based on accepted crater analysis techniques. The ultimate conclusion reached was that the mortar bomb in question could have been fired by either side in the conflict. Your Honours, that completes the summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. If you have any further questions for the witness, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, I do have some questions for you to follow-up on what you have in your written statement. If we can first look at page 1 and look at paragraph number 5. Here you state that you were team leader of the investigation. What would have been your precise role as the team leader?

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: My role would have been to provide direction to individual team members, to work with them initially to come up with a plan for the investigation, to oversee the conduct of the investigation, and then to work with the team to produce a report which I then delivered to the deputy force commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we move along to paragraph number 7 on this same page, you say that you were told to confine the investigation to crater analysis and related technical aspects of the explosion. What role, if any, did you have in confirming or refuting the number and nature of casualties?

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: That wasn't specifically explicitly part of our mandate.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And for purposes of the investigation that you were the team leader of, did you take into account any reports authored by the Bosnian police or government investigating the same incident?

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: I don't believe we received any reports from -- written reports from either side.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And had you had access to an -- to an available report from the Bosnian side, would you have used it for purposes of your investigation?

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: Based on evidence that I've given previously to investigators, I am aware that I had previously said to ICTY investigators that, hypothetically, if we had received reports from either side, we, I believe, would have been leery of such reports for fear that they would not be impartial and that they would need to be corroborated by independent evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now for purposes of the investigation which your team undertook, did you conduct any surveys of UNMOs on either side?

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: I believe we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And did you ever conduct an investigation to determine if anyone had heard the firing of the -- of a mortar?

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: I believe that was part of the questioning process for any UNMO or UNMO supervisors or other UN personnel that we interviewed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And did your team feel that either side of the conflict line could be excluded as the source of the fired round based on whether or not anyone heard it being fired?

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: Could you repeat the question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sure. Did your team feel that either side of the conflict line could be excluded as the source of the fired round based on whether or not anyone heard it being fired?

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And did your investigative team interview any civilians on the Bosnian side?

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: I don't believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: For purposes of the investigation that you were conducting, how would you have viewed any information from civilians if such was provided?

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: With some skepticism. Again, given everything that the civilians had been through, there would be a question about their impartiality with respect to a specific -- any specific incident. And again, we would have to have corroborated this with independent evidence. That was our feeling at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, could I ask one follow-up question here. Witness, did you understand the question of Mr. Ivetic to cover all civilians, whether Serb, Muslims, or foreigners, or were you in your answer specifically focusing on the population -- Muslim population residing in that part of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just to answer very specifically your question, we would have -- the answer that I gave previously applied to civilians, indigenous civilians, if I can use that term, whether they be Serb, Bosnian, whatever it might be. However, it would not apply to UN civilian employees. Of course, we would be prepared to take their testimony. So just to be clear on -- because there are some -- there were some civilians we would have had access to who were UN employees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did your investigative team determine the manufacturer or origin of manufacturing of the mortar shell that landed on the market-place at Markale?

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I can try to refresh your recollection, and if we can call up 1D6099 in e-court, and there should be a copy with the court reporter [sic] there with you. And this will be a statement from 24 July 2001 to it looks like Barry Hogan, Chester Stamp, and Richard Philipps. And if we could turn together to page 4, and if we could focus on the third paragraph from the top, and we see here, and I will read it into the record: "Our team considered whether the place of manufacture of the mortar bomb would have been significant, and we decided that it was not. The way the conflict was being conducted, with arms and ammunition being traded, purchased or captured by one side or another, from one side or another, made the origin of the mortar bomb a moot point. I don't believe that we followed up the manufacturer of the bomb because we didn't think it would prove anything. Similarly, the origin of the primer was not followed up for the same reasons." Sir, does that refresh your recollection as to the conclusions of your team as to investigating the manufacturing or origin of the mortar shell?

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: Yes, I recall reading this at -- previously, and I don't dispute saying it. I -- I accept the logic as it's portrayed in -- on paper. I simply could not recall whether or not we had made mention of this in our report. That's what I actually couldn't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Fair enough, then. We'll leave it at that and we'll get on to your report later. Now, if we can return now to the statement we looked at first, which is now D1242 marked for identification. And if we can turn to page 2, and if we could focus on paragraph number 9. In this paragraph, the method utilised by the 1st French Battalion team is described as being unconventional. Did any member of your team recognise this unconventional method as being a valid method?

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did your team take any steps to advise either the French Battalion or their commanders of the complaints as to their methodology?

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we turn to the last page of this statement, and first let's look at paragraph number 24, where you say both sides were known to have the type of mortar in question as well as the type of ammunition used. What can you tell us about the mobility of the mortar in question or lack thereof, whichever the case may be? How mobile is it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Objection to the form of the question. I believe it's a little compound and actually there is something inferred in the last part of it. Maybe if we could just have the witness explain something more straight-forward based on the actual paragraph itself. Just to be more particular, I read the paragraph as generally speaking about mortars of the sides and the question's calling it -- is referring to the mortar in question. That's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is a valid objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, would you please make a clear distinction between mortars -- general information as mortars used by the parties and the mortar which would have fired this projectile.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: How mobile are 120-millimetre mortars?

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: I am not an expert in 120-millimetre mortars. The point of paragraph 24 was to emphasize that ammunition -- mortar ammunition moved freely from one side to the other as ground was captured and so on. So the issue was more to do with the ammunition itself knowing that both sides used 120-millimetre mortars, so that the point of that paragraph was not to address the issue of mobility of the mortar equipment itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the interpreters ask the witness to bring the microphone closer. We can't hear him very well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Is this better?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: A little, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now I would like to take a look at Exhibit P538 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And that is the longer document that I sent along with the court officer. And before I ask you if you recognise the document, I would draw your attention to page 3 of the same which should have some signatures visible, and that might assist with the question of: Do you recognise this document.

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And do you recognise --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- what this document is?

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: Yes, it is a photocopy -- appears to be a copy of the investigation report that we produced in February of 1994, but I must say that the quality of this copy is not very good, and so we'll see as we go through it, but I just wanted to caution you that as it was printed here or appears here, it's worse than copies I've seen previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Agreed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could the microphone been adjusted again? It's not very well to be heard here on this side. Yes, I think it -- something like that. It was covered by the document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Is this better? How is this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It seems to be better. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I can advise you, sir, that we have the same bad copy on our side as well, so we'll work together through it and I think hopefully we can make use of it despite the apparent lack of clarity of certain parts of it. If we can go back --

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: Understood.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can go back to page 2, and it will be paragraph 10 of that document, page 2 in the English. It's the same page in B/C/S as we're at now, I think. And in the military analysis section, the phrase "known weapon positions" is used. To whom would this refer, known by whom?

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: UN Military Observers.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can move forward to the annexes of the report, and it will be page 34 in e-court. The assist the court officer at the videolink site, it's the page that has the ERN stamp at the top ending in 746. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And so here there should be a paragraph that says: "Conclusions." Is that the page that you have before you, sir?

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And here we have written: "The known BSA and Bih 120 mm mortar positions in the general area of interest are plotted at Appendix 1. It is clear from discussions with UNMOs and," it looks like MIOs, "that with their limited" --

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: That's --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: "... that with their limited freedom of movement and small number of observers, their knowledge of the details of 120 mm mortar positions and ammunition holdings in the area of interest is far from complete. Mortars are easy to hide and equally easy to move. From Appendix 1 it can be seen that the Serb position at Mrkovici is the nearest known position to the directional bracket. However, there could be any number of well-concealed 120 mm mortar positions which are unknown to UNPROFOR personnel on either side of the CL within the estimated range bracket. It can only be concluded from this assessment that, in theory, the fire could have originated from either side of the CL."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The problem is we don't have the B/C/S version on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Ah-ha.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Now it is there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now it's there. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: First of all, sir, does this refresh your recollection as to the conclusions of what was in the report of your investigative team?

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And do you agree with everything that is written here?

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now I want to look at just one more part of this same document.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It's labelled Annex 2 and would be page 39 in the English. To assist the Madam Registrar at the videolink room, the last four digits would be 4751. And so this will be four pages prior -- I'm sorry, four pages later in the B/C/S as well. So that will approximately 58. Okay. I think we're on the same page.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, do you have before you something that says "Annex 2" and then "Meeting Report"?

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: This appears to be a meeting with the Bosnian side discussing an investigation into Markale. So that we can refresh your recollection, if we skip two pages ahead to the page that has 4753 in the upper right-hand column, we see the participants listed, and that will be page -- there we go, in e-court, and we see that you are not listed as a participant. So the question I want to ask is: Do you recall if you ever personally met with the Bosnian Muslim side to discuss either your or their investigations into Markale?

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: Yes, I believe we met with liaison officers or representatives from each side, and I believe reports of those meetings are included in the report. This specific meeting that you refer to that you've just shown me was a meeting that was undertaken, I believe, by local UN forces prior to the convening of our investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your memory serves you well, sir. That's exactly, I think, accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now if we can go back one page prior -- and that will be -- the four-digit code at the end is 4752 there in the videolink room. And we'll need to go to the prior page in the B/C/S as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, you should have something there that starts off with Colonel Pardon and then has a paragraph underlined and bolded, saying: "General Conclusion." Is that the page that you are viewing in Canada?

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And here it is noted as follows: "It is to be noticed that during the whole meeting Bosnian declarations were aggressive at UNPROFOR general policy, blaming for its incompetence and lack of abilities of its members and accusing at several times that UN or UNPROFOR members often stated on Bosnian responsibility in the market shelling." Sir, did you come across or hear of the Bosnian side acting aggressively towards UNPROFOR or UN staff in relation to the investigations into the Markale shelling?

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And did you yourself know of any sentiments or talk within the UN or UNPROFOR based on a belief that the Bosnian side had responsibility in the market shelling?

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: Could you repeat the question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sure. Did you yourself know of any sentiments or talk within the UN or UNPROFOR which was based on a belief that the Bosnian side had its responsibility for the market shelling?

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: I don't recall any specific or useful information that would have helped us with the investigation in the context of what you've just said.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And what about within your investigative team itself? Was there any discussion of the Bosnian side being to blame for the incident?

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: Not to the best of my recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. General, I thank you for answering my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, that completes the direct examination. I've skipped some questions, so hopefully we have time to finish within today's frame.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think we'll be able to finish if -- certainly if Mr. Weber follows the same approach as you did, Mr. Ivetic, because you stayed well within the time limits you indicated before. Mr. Gauthier, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Weber. Mr. Weber is counsel for the Prosecution and you'll see him appear soon on your screen, I hope. Mr. Weber, you may --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can see him now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- proceed. That's even better. Mr. Weber, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Just a couple basic things before we get into some of the parts of your investigation. You previously testified in the Karadzic case in October 2012; correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And we've seen it once today, but just so we have it clearly on the record, you also provided a statement to an investigator named Barry Hogan in July of 2001; correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Between September 1993 and August of 1994, you were based in Zagreb, Croatia; right?

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your duties as force engineer in Zagreb included planning and providing safe accommodations for UN troops?

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: Yes, among many other things.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your responsibilities also included the -- securing the mobility of UN personnel across the mission area, and mine safety and clearance; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Let's go particularly to the Markale investigation. You arrived in Sarajevo on the 11th of February, 1994, after the shelling; correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Prior to February 1994, you actually had little or no experience in crater analysis; right?

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You had little or no experience in ballistics at the time of the Markale investigation?

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: However, as a trained engineer, a combat engineer, you did have experience with stationary explosives such as mines or other static explosives used to destroy, let's say, a bridge or a building; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: When you were assigned to the Markale investigation, the familiarity that you had with mortars came from training exercises dealing with the deployment of mortars in support of military operations; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: Yes, as well as general military training, but correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: We're agreed that mortars are area-suppressing anti-personnel weapons; right?

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Now, you've mentioned your report and we've looked -- we've seen it already once today, can you just confirm that your team completed its report setting out its findings on the 15th of February, 1994?

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And if you could please be handed Exhibit P538 again, the full report. General, also for the record, could you just please confirm that this is a copy of the final report that was completed by your team?

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: There were several annexes, and some of them have been mentioned today already, to the team's report. Could you please confirm that these are annexes A through G?

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: Do you want me to physically verify each of them? Is that -- are you asking me to verify that each of these is -- is attached to the report?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Well, the -- there are annexes A through G to the report. I know you might be reviewing your statement here, but if you are able to confirm that that is the complete report it would be appreciated.

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The final report and the annexes comprise the information that the team obtained during the course of your investigation as a whole; right?

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: As opposed to -- as a whole as opposed to --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I'll put it another way. It contained your complete findings and observations that your team acquired during the course of the investigation?

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: I believe so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Now, based upon your investigation and the report, I want to confirm a few of the -- a few things with you. First, could you confirm that your team concluded, based on its investigation, that the mortar shell in question had been launched in a conventional manner from a 120-millimetre mortar tube?

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The mortar exploded at ground level upon impact; right?

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The mortar did not impact a market stall or tabletop above the ground?

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your team found the crater shape to be consistent with the normal impact of a single mortar shell on an asphalt surface?

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your team assessed the direction of fire as being between 330 mils and 420 mils; correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The explosion was not caused by a stationary explosive device aboveground; correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could you explain to us the reasons that the explosion could not have been caused by a stationary explosive device?

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: The evidence which was recovered or observed by a number of subject matter experts, most notably, I would say, our explosive ordnance disposal expert, a Sergeant Dubant I believe his name was, made it very clear to him that this was very clearly a mortar, first of all; a 120-millimetre mortar, second of all; and that given the scrape pattern of shrapnel on the asphalt and the fuse tunnel and so on, that it -- it clearly was a mortar that had been fired with a fuse, I may not have the term exactly correct, but a fuse that had been fired by a firing pin. All of that evidence together made it clear that it wasn't a stationary bomb but that it was very definitely a mortar. And not just a mortar, but a 120-millimetre mortar.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your team also conclusively determined that the mortar was not hand-launched from a nearby building; right?

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your team did not rely on the findings of Captain Verdy and Major John Russell because they were shown to be inaccurate; correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You were aware that there were UNMOs on the -- UNMOs on the Bosnian side to the north-east of the impact area in February 1994 and they were able to move about as they wished?

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: On the Bosnian side, there were no fixed mortar positions along the direction of fire assessed by your team?

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: There were no known mortar positions along the assessed direction of fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your team did look into this; correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: Yes, but one of the issues, if both my memory and my reading of the report serve me correctly, is that there was freshly fallen snow at the time that -- that we did our investigation, which have -- which may have masked any signs of a mortar base plate position that might have been used to fire a mortar. And so for us to scour all of that terrain to try and determine where mortars might have been fired from and to -- then to narrow it down to a specific day that it would have been fired from was next to impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: And so we could not rule out that a mortar might have been fired by the Bosnian side, nor could we find evidence that it had been.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your team learned that in the territory held by the Bosnian Serb army that the assessed angle of fire or directional bracket fell within the area of responsibility of the Kosevo Brigade of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps; right?

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: I believe so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, do you not recall or -- if so, I can call up a past --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: -- statement of yours.

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: I -- to be absolutely certain, yes, you could take me back to that. I can recall reading that finding sometime in the last 24 hours in my report, but where specifically and what specifically it said, I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 33079, e-court page 11. For the court officer there, I will be referring to transcript page 29417.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar informs me that the document has not yet been released, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Stewart, it has been released? I see you're nodding "yes." Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Your Honour, could the counsel repeat? The number was 33079?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, this is your transcript of your previous testimony in the Karadzic proceedings. I'd like to direct your attention to line 12. The question posed to you: "And your team did learn that in Bosnian Serb army-held territory that the assessed angle of fire or the directional bracket fell within the area of responsibility of the Kosevo Brigade of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps?" Your answer was: "Yes, that's correct." Do you stand by this testimony?

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: Could you just tell me which page I'm supposed to be on?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, I'm referring you to transcript page, which is going to be in the upper right-hand corner for you, of 29417.

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I agree with -- my answer to your previous question is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: This area was assessed to be in the area of Mrkovici; correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your team did identify mortar positions in the territory of the Bosnian Serb army in the directional bracket of fire; right?

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see that we're almost at the time for the break. I'm about to head into one last topic, if we could take the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll take the break now. Mr. Tieger, you're on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, just a quick housekeeping matter. Today was the day the Court was -- in which I was to respond to the Trial Chamber's invitation concerning the provisional projection for rebuttal. I raise that now because I didn't want to interfere with the timing on the videolink, but I have a preexisting presentation from 4.15 to 5.15. So I -- I raise that so the Court can either determine whether it wants to ask me to make the submissions at the end of next session or if -- if you're going to continue beyond 5.15 or if you just want to defer it to tomorrow, but I wanted to let you know that I was prepared to do that but had this scheduling difficulty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll think it over. How much time would you need to make those submissions?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If there are no questions from the Court, probably about five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Approximately about five minutes. Then I suggest to do the following, that we give a little bit extra time to the witness to read again his statement and to see whether any corrections are needed, so that we therefore would continue after a 20-minute break first for five minutes, just The Hague, and then restore the videolink and continue with the testimony of the witness. Because I think we are ahead of schedule anyhow due to the fact that Mr. Ivetic took considerably less time than announced. Then we'll take a break and we would expect the videolink to be restored in 25 minutes from now, that would be at local The Hague time 3.30, but we'll resume, however, at local The Hague time 3.25.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. As the Court will recall, on the 17th of August, the Chamber invited the Prosecution to give a provisional indication of whether, what kind, and how much rebuttal evidence it intends to present. I hope my submissions this afternoon are within the spirit of the Court's inquiry. First, let me note that we understood the use of the term "provisional" to reflect the fact that there are still witnesses remaining, including many experts, and also that the Prosecution has not received, much less reviewed, expected bar table submissions from the Defence. And while those factors clearly give rise to the possibility of additions to our current assessment, they also give rise to the possibility that the evidence adduced during the course of direct or cross-examinations during the remaining process may also give rise to reductions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think you understood the reason why we said "provisional" very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So in that connection we are happy to offer a provisional indication, that we do expect to be seeking rebuttal, but also a simultaneous representation that we expect that to be extremely modest in scope. And indeed even within that modest scope, the bulk of the anticipated rebuttal should have no impact on court time because it deals with paper issues outside of court. So let me put some quick numbers and characterisations to that that bear out that assessment. So first, by way of example, we would anticipate the submission of a certain number of documents, at least at this stage, but at this stage we put those on the order of some 20 to 50 or so, if that helps the Court in its anticipations. Secondly, I would focus on an issue or a mechanism closely related to rebuttal that pretty much overlaps but is a mechanism different from a rebuttal motion, and that refers to the portions of statements that were redacted due to overlap with adjudicated facts in instances where adjudicated facts have been challenged. But because we consider that a challenge must be grounded on credible evidence to have any impact on an adjudicated fact, we are considering only a tiny handful of instances, two to three. However, in those circumstances, we consider at this point that the proper procedural mechanism would be a motion for reconsideration rather than rebuttal; that is, it would be based on the fact that in that particular process the redaction order was grounded on an adjudicated fact, and then the challenge to that adjudicated fact represents a change in circumstance justifying reconsideration. More importantly, for purposes of this discussion, the particular two to three we have in mind are from 92 bis statements. And so I'm not quite certain that the procedural mechanism is of such moment to the Court right now, but I wanted to foreshadow that. We are also considering two 92 quater statements. And finally, the only aspect of the provisional rebuttal assessment that seems to implicate court time would be our consideration at the moment of two viva voce witnesses, but based on our assessment, those witnesses would not consume more than three days of court time for both direct and cross-examination. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For the two --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: For the two together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And in any event, we are -- as I say, we will still be considering all of those factors, frankly, in the hope of reducing it even further as the case continues until such point as the Court indicates a formal motion should be filed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. Before we continue with the videolink, I think that the Defence had announced that the time for the witness to be called tomorrow would be double the number, that's ten hours instead of five. The Chamber has not yet decided that it would grant such a request for double time, and the Defence is invited to organise its examination-in-chief in such a way that the most relevant parts would come first and we'll then consider whether or not we'll grant any additional time. There is already a huge number of pages of reports involved and then the day before the examination to double the time is something that needs more attention. And therefore, please focus on what is most important to start with, and then we'll see where we are after five hours. Mr. Weber, I think that the -- the Prosecution indicated that it would need 16 instead of 8 hours, or is it double --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: No, no. Your Honour, our estimate is kept at 8 hours right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: So not doubling the estimate as of right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I don't know -- can't foresee everything that happens, but...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course we never know. But there is clear guidance now for the Defence to see whether they can stick to their original time limits and at least convince the Chamber, by the relevance of all the evidence elicited, that there is really a reason to need more time than the five hours as indicated earlier. I leave it to that, but we didn't want to leave it until tomorrow so that at least the Defence has an opportunity to further prepare for that next witness. Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, since we are discussing the next witness, just one related matter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: -- so that we can deal with it at one time. I just wanted to note that for the noticed exhibits for the next witness, not all the 65 ter numbers are uploaded -- well, they may be uploaded but they are not released to us right now. So as a matter of urgency, if the Defence could please make sure that they are all released. We do note that not all the materials are on the Defence 65 ter list, and while we -- generally this is not a problem and we do have the reports, we don't know fully all the significance of all the materials at this time, and we -- this could raise some issues as to good cause and relate to the significance --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: -- and the relevance of the materials, but we'll address those as it comes up, but I just wanted to raise this issue at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and whether you need to know because of tendering and a decision on admission, you would also need to know in order to know whether the 65 ter list could be expanded by adding new documents. I take it that this message is well received and that the Defence takes care of it without delay. Then we return to what we were doing today, that is, to hear the evidence of Mr. Gauthier. First of all, could the representatives of the Canadian government, but without any problem, enter the videolink room together with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Welcome back, Mr. Gauthier. Before we continue, did you have an opportunity to re-read your statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any need to correct anything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then I think that nothing opposes admission. Madam Registrar, the number was?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D1242, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1242 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: During the investigation, you learned that Colonel Cvetkovic from the VRS stated that the Kosevo Brigade had mortar positions including a 120-millimetre mortar in the Mrkovici area; right?

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You personally met with Colonel Cvetkovic on the 13th of February, 1994; right?

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Did you know that Colonel Cvetkovic was a commander of an artillery regiment which had been tasked, prior to the Markale shelling, with providing fire support from Mrkovici as part of offensive activities; were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Neither you nor members of your team went to visit these mortar positions; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You were aware that UNMOs had been denied freedom of movement to the Bosnian Serb army positions in the assessed direction of fire since October 1993; correct?

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Weber. Before we continue, I think that the number of the statement is 1242 rather than what now appears at this moment in the transcript. I should have said what now appeared on the transcript. Mr. Ivetic --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I have just a few --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -any questions in re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I have just a few questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gauthier, Mr. Ivetic will put a few more questions to you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, you were asked about Major Russell's assessment being inaccurate. Do you recall what part of the analysis or assessment of Major Russell was said to be inaccurate?

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: I would have to go back and look at the evidence that I've provided previously to refresh my memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And were you aware of Major Russell amending his assessment at a date subsequent to your report to exclude his previous opinion that the shell had struck a table?

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: No, I was not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you have any opinion as to -- well, strike that. Since you are not aware of that amended assessment, do you have any opinion as to the accuracy or inaccuracy of that amended assessment that came after your report?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Objection --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can only --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. -- one second, please. Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Objection, calls for speculation. It's also not clear that -- what we are talking about or not talking about and what the witness is commenting on. He's not indicated any knowledge of the event -- of the event being referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, the witness is called as a witness of fact and you are bluntly asking for his opinion on -- and that's may be another issue, on someone else amending his assessment of which the witness is not aware. So therefore, I take it that he is also not aware of the reasons why he reviewed his initial assessment. Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- if you want to deal with the matter, then do it in a very systemic way. Try to avoid opinion. Although the witness, of course, has given on a few matters opinions as well. So I'm not in every respect stopping you from doing that, but to ask someone's opinion about someone else who changed his opinion where this witness is even unaware of how and how and why he changed his opinion, that's not something I think that would assist the Chamber. So if you want to proceed on opinions, do it very cautiously and very precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution asked this witness his opinion of Major Russell's report, and he gave an answer in cross-examination. They did not identify which of Major Russell's reports is at issue. That is what I am trying to determine in exploring with the witness right now because as we know from Major Russell's testimony, there was a second amendment that was done after the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But this witness may not be aware of any, and so therefore if you want to ask him anything about that, then it should be presented to him in a way which makes it clear that at least he knows what he is confronted with at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think I can do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, when you answered the Prosecution's question as to Major Russell's report, to which report of Major Russell were you making reference to?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I'm going to object. I don't believe I used the word "report."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's see. Mr. Ivetic, could you guide us to exactly which page -- I see Mr. Russell appears on page 23, 34, and 35. Could you -- I think that --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I referred to findings. I didn't particularize a particular report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's see, Mr. Ivetic, you have a certain matter on your mind. Could you assist the Chamber by telling us what portion exactly you had in mind when, as you said, the Prosecution asked for ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I can, page 23 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- line 5 through 7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I have that now before me. The question then was: "Your team did not rely on the findings of Captain Verdy and Major John Russell because they were shown to be inaccurate; correct?" And the answer was: "Correct." So you're referring to that. As a matter of fact, the witness wasn't asked for any opinion. It was whether they did rely or not. That's not a matter of opinion but that's a matter of fact. But again, I'm not stopping you, but let's be very accurate and precise in this context. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm trying to, Your Honour. And it says: "... because they were shown to be inaccurate; correct?" That was the question asked. So with all due respect, it is asking opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think as a matter of fact that that's even part of the statement of the witness, isn't it? That's -- Verdy certainly is as with mathematical errors. So therefore that's already in the statement. That's not asking in itself for opinion. Here Mr. Weber has asked whether they did not rely for the reasons shown. That's a composite question. Better, it would have been to say, first, did you not rely --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Agreed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- second, was it for that reason that you did not rely, and those both are questions of fact. But again I said I will not stop you at this moment as long as you are accurate on the matter. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in your written statement that we have introduced today as D1242, in paragraph number 12 and 13, you talk about a crater analysis performed by Major Russell, and you talk about a copy in 13 of the memorandum which he had entitled "Amplification of crater analysis of 5 February 1994, Sarajevo market." In your answer to the Prosecution's question, were you talking about any findings of Major Russell apart from that which is contained in paragraphs 12 and 13 of your statement?

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: I would have to refresh my memory by also looking at the statement that I made to the ICTY investigators in 2001, where I do recall being asked again about Major Russell's evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we can turn to 1D6099 in e-court, and that is the statement given to the investigators of the Tribunal. And if we could turn to page 3, and if we could focus on the fifth paragraph from the bottom. It's right in the middle.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And it says: "Referring to document numbered 0026-4142 ..." Are we at the same page, sir?

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And here it says: "Referring to document numbered 0026-4142 through 0026-4144, we had that document during our investigation and we did interview Major Russell. Some of his findings were inconsistent with ours, and we disproved such findings as his claim that the round had impacted a vendor's table. I think that the reason we did not specifically refute Major Russell's report was that he had not done an official investigation." Does that refresh your recollection as to Major Russell's findings?

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And do you stand by what is written in this statement given to the investigators of the Tribunal as to what -- as to those findings and as to what you found to be inaccurate?

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now in -- if we return now to the original question. Apart from this memorandum, whose ERN numbers we have just read and which had a finding that the round had impacted on a vendor's table, were your comments to the Prosecution in cross-examination about the inaccuracy of Major Russell's findings related to anything else, any other reports or findings of Major Russell, or is this the document that we are talking about?

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: You're -- you just asked me two questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Let's start with the first one. In your comments to the Prosecution in cross-examination about the inaccuracy of Major Russell's findings, to what did they relate, now having been refreshed with what we looked at?

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: They relate to the fact that Major Russell had concluded that the round had impacted a vendor's table, but they also relate to the fact that he had -- he had established an angle of descent between 1200 and 1300 mils, which was much more precise than our findings.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And with respect to the measuring of the angle of descent, who measured first sequentially? Was it your team or Major Russell?

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: Major Russell.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And do you know if anything else was done in respect to the crater hole in between Major Russell's measuring and the measuring performed by your team?

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: I can't say for certain if anything had been done before or after -- actually, I can't remember the sequence. I do remember vaguely that Major Russell was not the first person on the scene.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we can now return just briefly to your other statement, that is D1 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have you done with the subject matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Or is it -- are you still on the same? Then I'll wait for a second. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could return to D1242, and page 3 of the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in paragraph 20, you state that: "Some members of our team made estimates of the angle of descent based upon the crater at the time of our investigation ..." And you give two such estimates by Major Khan and Commandant Hamill. And then it would appear that Captain Grande and Sergeant Chef Dubant did not believe it possible to make an estimate because of the fact that the crater had been excavated and slightly enlarged and also since the crater had been re-dug in order to extract the tail fin. So when you said that the measurements of Major Russell were more precise than your own findings, are these the findings that you are talking about? The ones that are contained in paragraph 20?

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: If I can just clarify, when I say "precise," I mean that he -- he is very specific. I don't mean precise in terms of being more accurate. I mean more specific, so bracketed to 1200 to 1300 mils. Whereas in our investigation and our conclusions, we, I believe, had found that to pin-point would depend on -- on a knowledge of which charge was used. I could be wrong on that, but that -- but I did mean "specific" rather than "precise."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Then that addresses what I was asking you, and I thank you for that clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, that is all I have on that topic and also for redirect, so if Your Honours had another question you're free to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I think you dealt with most of it, but let me re-read the answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm still puzzled a bit, Mr. Gauthier, by your answer about precision. I see in your report that Russell stated the angle of descent between 1200 and 1300; Khan came up with 1000 to 1100; and Hamill with 950 to 100. So the range for all three of them is more or less a hundred or a hundred-plus mils as -- as the range in which they are not certain. Now, you say you would have to know the charge used. I do understand that the charge used may have an effect on the angle of descent, but would you agree with me that you could assess or even establish the angle of descent without knowing at all what charge was used?

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: Yes, I think in thinking my way through the answer I may have conflated two different issues; one being the angle of descent, and the other being the estimation of the distance from the target.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I now do --

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: And so -- right. So I was actually thinking about there were various possibilities in terms of the distance from the target, and that's what was in my mind was that there would be a number of them; whereas the angle of descent is the angle of descent and there would only be one of those estimated by a particular individual. So you are correct, Your Honour. That was my error.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you for that answer. I have one other question for you. In paragraph 9 of your statement, you say that FreBat 4 team used an unconventional method, and then you describe two methods, the one you considered conventional and the other one as unconventional. My first question would be: The unconventional method, is there any reason to believe that what is unconventional is worse or less reliable?

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: Yes, I believe so. And again, this is from memory to a certain extent, but I believe we used the term "unconventional" to mean inconsistent with accepted practices. And it is not -- there is an accepted way of doing a crater analysis, and to determine the bearing, as noted in the statement, you would try and fix two points along the line --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let me, if you wouldn't mind, to stop you there. Could you be very precise, because I tried to understand what you meant by "two points along a line." I do not know yet how you determine the points, I do not know what line you are referring to, so could you be very detailed and precise in describing both the methods, the conventional one to start with and later then the other one? You say "fixing two points along a line," what line?

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: The line would be the bearing from north, the bearing or line -- effectively a horizontal line drawn between the target, in this case the -- the centre of the crater and from there back to the estimated point of launching of the firing of the mortar. So that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you draw --

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: -- is the line you're referring to, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're drawing -- if I may stop you to make sure that I fully understand. You say you draw a line between the centre of the crater --

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- to where you think the shell was fired from. So that is at that point in --

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- time you assume that the shell is fired from a certain -- and then you draw between in that direction --

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- from the centre of the crater. Okay, that's the line, yes. And how do you choose then your two points?

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Just to be clear, you are not assuming a point. You are estimating the line, and that line would be from the centre of the crater back to the firing point, but you are not assuming the location of this firing point. You are using this to estimate that line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, because you don't know yet. Because the whole exercise is finally --

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- aiming at to establish --

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- where it was. So it can be an assumption on -- perhaps on the basis of what you see on the ground as the pattern. Is that the pattern of shrapnel?

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: Yes, yes, exactly right. And so -- yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Now we have drawn that line between the centre of the crater in the direction where you suspect the origin of fire is on the basis of what you find as a pattern of shrapnel impact on the surface.

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: Yes. By looking at the pattern that will give you -- by actually -- it's almost like a compass, where you trace the pattern to get to a point, and you trace from one side and you trace from the other side to give you a point on the ground. And so that point on the ground, the line between that point on the ground and the centre of the crater would give you two points along the line from which you could estimate the line from which -- the point from which the mortar was fired.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it's still not entirely clear to me how you fix that second point. How is that exactly done?

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: If my memory serves me correctly, it was done with two rods, I believe. So you use a rigid rod from the point of the crater, and another along the -- what is estimated to be the general line -- there is a pattern formed by the scrape from the -- the shrapnel, and that -- that allows you to go in an arch which essentially it's -- it forms an arc, and then you do the same thing on the other side which forms another arc, and the point where the two arcs meet becomes the common point between the two. And again, this is all -- Your Honour, you'll have to forgive me, but this is from memory and I'm not a technical expert, and so it is my recollection of how this was actually done when I observed different teams doing the crater analysis. So they were able to draw these two arcs along the shrapnel pattern, and those two arcs intersect at a certain point. And it was that intersecting point that was used as the second point in the line --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: -- to give you the bearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, this all depends on where you put these rigid rods where you start making that arch, because that would define where the two would meet. How do you --

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: Certainly, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How do you determine where to start with this exercise with the two rods to find where they meet when moving them? Could you tell us how you define that initial point for those two rods?

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: I'm assuming the fuse tunnel. In the crater there is a hole at the bottom that I suppose is deep enough that it's -- it's reasonably clear where that -- where that hole is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: -- and a rod is actually stuck into the hole. Again, if my -- if my memory serves me correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But then later -- first of all, you are talking about one rod and earlier you said where the two rods meet. And the starting point for your line was already the centre of the crater, so I'm a bit puzzled by how it really works.

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: Well -- but that's -- that's what I'm referring to, the hole in the ground is the centre of the crater. And I just -- to be honest, I cannot clearly remember what tools were used to actually trace out the arc. I do remember that an arc was traced from both sides. The instruments that were used to trace out the arc I just don't remember. I'm afraid I don't remember, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, since you refer to it was done from both sides, I asked you how you would determine the starting point from doing that exercise from both sides, and in your answer you took me back to the centre of the crater. That confused me slightly because it's not from both sides anymore but it comes from the centre of the crater.

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: I'm wondering, Your Honour, if it would be easier if we used one of the diagrams in Sergeant Dubant's statement which is attached to the investigation report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would be quite willing to do so, but I must admit that I don't have them by hand. Perhaps the parties could assist.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That should be P538. And I believe the -- Dubant's part is the second English file that is -- that comprises that exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we have --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: But, Your Honours, I would just suggest that maybe just visually it may be better to have the witness possibly look at the ERN ending in 737 or 738.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, now that's fine if you want to do that in re-examination, but the witness suggested to look at something he thought would assist him. And let's --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That is also Dubant's part [overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And I believe that is part of Dubant's part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you say let him do something else which is, by the way, the same. Yes, okay. That's just a matter of understanding. Could we have the report -- what was it? 538 on our screens, P538. Is this 538 what we have on our screens at this moment? And then we go to page --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: 25, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes, I was suggesting either e-court page 25 or 26.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Or in fact 27, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if that assists you better, then -- 27 is tables, if I see that well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, we're not speaking of the same -- it's this one here. I'm not sure which reference number you're using --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it the one --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Your Honour, the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] The witness is looking at page that ends with the four digits 4738 of the ERN number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And I think what we should look at 4737, unless the witness would disagree.

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: 47 --4738 [Overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 4738, yes, now --

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: -- actually is very good.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see. We have now --

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: It's not consistent with what I said previously, but it does provide the two points.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please kindly not overlap.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I asked you to repeat what you just said, Witness. You made a comment but there were overlapping speakers. Could you repeat what you just said.

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: Yes, I apologise, Your Honour. The diagram that I am looking at very clearly shows that the two points with the intersections of the arcs, it's not consistent with what I had described but that simply suggests that my memory is not that good. But it does show in a sense the centre of the crater with the shrapnel pattern, and it shows how Sergeant Dubant, in this case, came to his determination of a bearing of 355 mils. And I'm afraid I -- and it may be explained also in his written report. I cannot look at this diagram and tell you precisely what instruments were used in what way to derive the two points, but you can see from the diagram that there are effectively arcs that intersect and give you, in fact, two points in addition to the centre of the crater to give you that bearing of 355 millimetres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So connecting the two points is the connection between the two points that goes through the centre of the crater.

utterances.speaker: MICHEL GAUTHIER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
